claims.text: High-throughput experimental screening using thermogravimetry can be used to study high-temperature oxidation behavior in nickel-based alloys.
High-throughput experimental screening using thermogravimetry can be used to study phase stability in nickel-based alloys.
The proposed initial material is a polycrystalline, annealed nickel-based alloy such as Inconel 718.
The alloy is oxidized in air at 900°C for 100 hours.
The proposed isothermal oxidation test uses a heating rate of 10°C/min.
Oxidation produces a protective oxide scale, exemplified by Cr2O3.
The oxide scale grows by a diffusion-controlled mechanism.
Diffusion-controlled oxide-scale growth leads to parabolic oxidation kinetics.
The annealed alloy is predicted to have a 30% lower oxidation rate than the same alloy in the as-cast condition.
A 30% reduction from 0.5 mg/cm²/h corresponds to a predicted oxidation rate of 0.35 mg/cm²/h.
As-cast Inconel 718 has a baseline oxidation rate of 0.5 mg/cm²/h at 900°C.
An oxidation rate below 0.35 mg/cm²/h indicates improved high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The measured oxidation rate may depend on alloy composition, surface finish, and testing conditions.
TGA with simultaneous DSC can measure mass change and heat flow during the proposed test.
The hypothesis is designated as falsified if the measured oxidation rate exceeds 0.45 mg/cm²/h.

contradictions.description: The predicted 30% reduction from 0.5 mg/cm²/h equals 0.35 mg/cm²/h, but improvement is defined strictly as a rate below 0.35 mg/cm²/h; therefore, the predicted value does not satisfy the stated improvement criterion.

The mechanism specifies parabolic oxidation kinetics, but the outcome and baseline are expressed as constant rates in mg/cm²/h. Parabolic kinetics ordinarily require a time-dependent rate or a parabolic rate constant, so these quantities are not internally aligned.
